items.title: The GOP’s Message to Immigrants
items.description: Only a few decades ago, Republican presidents would happily evoke the idea of America as a haven for people around the world. Ronald Reagan, in his farewell speech, declared that “anyone, from any corner of the Earth, can come to live in America and become an American.” Reagan was no paragon of racial tolerance—he opposed the civil-rights movement and privately referred to Black people as “ monkeys ”—but he did not regard the presence of nonwhite people as an existential threat to America. For years the Republican Party insisted that what it wanted was a certain kind of immigrant—highly skilled people who came here legally, or even, not that long ago, those brought to the U.S. as children who lacked status through no fault of their own and had long since assimilated. That Republican Party no longer exists. Today the GOP’s view is that almost all immigration—by which the Trump administration seems to mean nonwhite immigration, euphemistically referred to as “Third World” immigration—is bad. That view can be summed up by Homeland Security’s celebratory announcement on X last week that the country was seeing a decline in naturalizations, as if the decline itself were self-evidently a good thing: “Net negative migration for the first time in HALF a CENTURY. Americans are amassing victories NEVER seen before thanks to President Trump.” The “right” kind of immigrant seems to have become a much narrower category, one defined not by people’s education, potential, or ties to the country, but simply by whether they are white and Christian. A recent Fox News headline exulted : “Republican Glee Erupts as White House Boasts Sharp Decline in Immigration From Muslim-Majority Nations.” These people could be doctors, engineers, or artists, but if they’re from a “Muslim-majority country,” these Republicans don’t want them here. And this week, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin posted that “socialists”—by which he presumably meant leftists sympathetic to immigrants—want to “vandalize American demographics to gain political power.” This is the language of racial purity, and it is not a concept that confines itself to immigration. It suggests that Americans who do not fit the Trump administration’s preferred “demographics” do not belong. In the many parts of the United States where the native-born population is declining, communities desperately need immigrants. This is true in areas of Ohio, where Haitian immigration has contributed to an economic revival . But to President Trump, Haiti is a “shithole” country, and all Haitians are invaders to be expelled. To that end, the administration removed the Temporary Protected Status that had allowed Haitian immigrants to stay in the United States, and in July, Haitians in Ohio began being fitted with ankle monitors. Pierre Damas Bel was in college at Wright State University in Ohio when he was issued his bulky ankle monitor. He was an athlete. And he hoped to study neuroscience and be a doctor. He was exactly the kind of young person whom previous versions of the Republican Party would have seen as an American success story. But he was a Haitian immigrant, so he was not wanted by the Trump administration, which did not seem to care who he was, or who he might become. In September, he called his father to say he felt “humiliated.” CNN reported that soon after, police told his father that he had “thrown himself under a truck.” A local pastor, Carl Ruby, said at a news conference that it was “our immigration policy that took his life.” [ Read: A reckoning in Springfield ] A year ago, The New York Times obtained documents submitted to the president by officials at the Departments of State and Homeland Security claiming that “the sharp increase in diversity has reduced the level of social trust essential for the functioning of a democratic polity,” and arguing that the U.S. should admit only “refugees who can be fully and appropriately assimilate [ sic ], and are aligned with the president’s objectives.” We now know what was meant by this. The Trump administration has turned refugee admissions into a virtually whites-only program for Afrikaners from South Africa. The applications of these so-called refugees—who do not face significant levels of persecution—are being processed quickly, while those of other groups around the world have largely been suspended. The administration portrays most immigrants as people who leech off U.S. taxpayers rather than contributing, but it has supported South Africans in this whites-only refugee program at taxpayer expense. The Afrikaner policy is illuminating, because it proves the catch-22 facing nonwhite immigrants: If you are poor, you are a moocher, and if you are gainfully employed, you are taking a job from a hardworking American. The only way to be a good immigrant is to be white and Christian. Bo French, who is running for a seat on the Texas Railroad Commission, has taken this idea a step further, suggesting that the only way to be an American is to be white and Christian. Last month, French responded to a photograph of Asian students cheering the University of Texas football team by posting, “I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn’t believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined,” adding that “social media is exposing how many Americans have been displaced by foreigners.” French later said, “I think that the bigger conversation is, are we going to have policies that prioritize Americans, and the exceptionalism that I believe Americans have, or are we going to have policies that prioritize foreigners?” State law requires that 90 percent of UT’s students be from Texas; only 10 percent can be international or out-of-state students. French had no idea of the citizenship status of the young people in the photo. What made the students “foreigners” to French was that they were not white. The conservative activist Christopher Rufo discussed French’s comments on a podcast with Jonathan Keeperman, who leads a book publisher of conservative titles. Keeperman explained that “the mere fact of us being able to notice that No, this is not an assimilated group, this is just a bunch of Indians at the game is itself sort of definitionally the case that they’re not yet assimilated.” What makes them not assimilated? Nothing more than the opinion of a guy who looks at a picture and sees, as Keeperman put it, “just a bunch of Indians.” It is difficult to imagine a behavior more indicative of assimilation than rejoicing in the victory of your college football team in Texas. And that’s the point: Assimilation is no longer about going to school, getting a job, speaking English, and embracing local culture. It’s about being white and Christian. In recent years, many conservatives have championed a kind of reactionary “color-blindness” that insists that any race-conscious effort to alleviate discrimination is itself equivalent to racial discrimination. White people earned their success, this argument assumes, but people in all other groups were given unfair advantages—a notable inversion of American history. Affirmative action has been struck down by the Supreme Court, and offices promoting diversity, equity, and inclusion have been restricted or outlawed at public universities in many states, including Texas. But the success of nonwhite people remains suspect. In fact, that success is evidence that something is deeply wrong with the system. As my colleague Jonathan Chait wrote about the Rufo and Keeperman podcast, “Resentment of these immigrant communities is understandable, the two men explained, not in spite of the fact that so many South Asians have been successful academically and economically, but because of it.” If “meritocracy” does not produce an overwhelming white majority in elite spaces such as Texas’s flagship public university, what good is it? Color-blind meritocracy was, for many years, a successful rhetorical strategy for undermining antidiscrimination law and excluding Black people from selective schools and prominent positions. That’s why so many former segregationists seemed to suddenly embrace the concept in the 1970s. For them, resegregation —not color-blindness—was always the goal. As long as the success of some immigrants could be used to paint Black students as undeserving, color-blind meritocracy was good. But now many on the right see a new problem: too many Asian Americans in elite spaces. Their success, therefore, must be portrayed as a sinister theft of real (white) Americans’ birthright. [ Jonathan Chait: The mainstreaming of anti-Indian bigotry ] The declining “social trust” that the administration warned against is, of course, not the fault of these students. The problem is bigots like Bo French who cannot accept into their community people who do not share their race and religion, and those who monetize or otherwise profit from that bigotry by spreading it through social media. Like the proverbial child who kills their parents and asks for mercy as an orphan, they are responsible for the problem they are decrying. Perhaps more significant than French’s remarks is that few Republican politicians in Texas were willing to criticize them. Governor Greg Abbott, who has endorsed French, distanced himself but did not condemn the remarks. Neither did Texas Lieutenant Governor Dan Patrick. Nor did Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton , who is running for a U.S. Senate seat. Senator John Cornyn, who lost the primary to Paxton, was among the few sitting Republican officeholders who did, saying French was “an embarrassment to the Republican Party, and he’s going to drag the whole ticket down because of his racist comments.” One wonders whether he would have felt free to speak so frankly had he not been primaried out of his seat. The former Bush adviser Karl Rove, hardly a liberal squish, complained that “my party is being infiltrated by people like Bo French. Nick Fuentes goes to Dallas and meets with a bunch of Republican leaders. This guy is a Nazi.” I’m afraid that these people have not “infiltrated” the Republican Party. Today, they are the Republican Party.

items.title: What Trump’s Chatbot Told Me About the Election
items.description: A round the same time that the world learned that swarms of autonomous AI agents were escaping their testing environments and carrying out sophisticated hacking attacks this past summer, researchers who focus on election security were running tests of their own. They wanted to see whether the safeguards that top AI companies had enacted to prevent their technology from disrupting the upcoming midterms would work in the real world. The results were ominous. In response to sample prompts designed to create misinformation, several chatbots produced realistic photos of a man stuffing ballots into a mailbox, a man holding a foreign passport while trying to vote, and FBI agents investigating a voter-registration organization. The chatbots also created fraudulent government documents and deepfake videos of government officials purporting to substantiate election-conspiracy theories. In some cases, the chatbots acted in violation of their own policies. They even helped the researchers, from the Brennan Center for Justice, hone the prompts that would create propaganda to boost specious claims of election fraud. The resulting images were so realistic that when the researchers asked other chatbots to determine whether they were real or fake, several of the leading AI firms’ models were stumped. Much of the activity contravened safety systems that companies had touted just months ago—and some seemed to run afoul of various state laws, researchers found. The experiment shows just how wide the gap has become between the fast-moving technology and the glacially paced effort to regulate it, Lawrence Norden, who helped conduct the research as the Brennan Center’s vice president of elections and government, told me. “All the companies apparently have some guardrails to try to prevent this from happening,” he said, citing AI firms’ written guidelines around misinformation and cybersecurity. “They’re easily circumventable, and the tools themselves make it easy to circumvent them. That’s really what makes me think we’re not ready.“ Washington and Silicon Valley have been consumed in recent weeks with debate over the extent to which ever more intelligent AI agents may put all of humanity in danger . Much less attention has been on what researchers and election officials told me is a more pressing short-term reality: The November midterms are more vulnerable to AI-powered disruption or manipulation than most voters realize. Few signs indicate that the federal government is taking the risks as seriously as it should. Instead, as misinformation and cyberhacking threats rise, the agencies and entities responsible for protecting America’s electoral infrastructure have been gutted, downgraded, or otherwise neutralized. As a result, the 2026 midterms are shaping up to be the first live, real-world test of whether the jumble of state, local, and industry policies designed to protect against a breakdown in election systems can hold up in the AI era. Few election and cybersecurity experts believe that this patchwork is well suited to stopping a serious attack. [ Read: Trump’s see-no-evil AI policy ] Such attacks could be carried out in different ways. Sophisticated misinformation campaigns using the latest generative technology could convince voters that the election has been compromised. Election officials are also concerned that AI-assisted cyberattacks could take down critical voting infrastructure. There is little evidence that AI agents would have the ability to infiltrate vote-counting systems to manipulate actual votes, which are almost always backed up by a paper record. T he breaches of the AI company Hugging Face and attempted hacks of government agencies by rogue agents in recent months have led companies to pause some AI development, call for new regulations, and implement measures to counter the mounting risks to public safety. There are few signs that the technology’s threats to election security are creating a similar level of caution. Some state and local officials, with little guidance from the federal government, are scrambling to prepare for a range of unpredictable scenarios, Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows told me. The tools available to malicious actors are rapidly improving, forcing government officials to play catch-up. “As we think about the threat of AI, we think about deepfakes; we think about bots, hacking, and disrupting our official websites or bringing down essential voter-registration systems,” Bellows said. “It means that we have to work even harder to protect ourselves.” The Brennan Center study​​—and similar tests run this year by other organizations, including the pro-democracy group States United—found that it has become easy for AI to create confusion before, during, and after an election. In one instance, researchers used a publicly available AI tool to reproduce a version of a disinformation video created in Russia and released in the lead-up to the 2024 U.S. presidential election. “The ease with which we created this video—which, in the past, would have required actors, cameras, and production infrastructure—illustrates the power of modern chatbots to generate misinformation easily and prolifically,” the Brennan Center researchers wrote in their August report . Brennan Center An AI-generated image from the Brennan Center study shows a man casting a ballot while holding a foreign passport. Brennan Center An AI-generated image Brennan Center researchers created with ChatGPT that they say appears to show a person instructing people how to fill out their ballots. The chatbots did provide some guardrails. When researchers posed as election skeptics and tried to prompt various chatbots to confirm a series of conspiracy theories, the models consistently tried to debunk such claims. The States United probe found that the models improved their accuracy over time, and ChatGPT and Google AI both became markedly more accurate in answering election-related inquiries from late 2025 to early 2026. At the same time, chatbots’ inclination to be friendly—and occasionally sycophantic—sometimes led to banter that appeared to validate false ideas about election fraud. “That feeling you can’t put your finger on? It was put there deliberately by people who raised hundreds of millions of dollars off it,” Anthropic’s Claude told a Brennan Center researcher who posed as a user with doubts about the 2020 election. “Questioning elections is American as apple pie,” xAI’s Grok told another researcher. The study’s authors were often able to bypass safeguards that AI companies had set up to prevent their agents from producing election-related misinformation, either by changing the settings or by switching among different AI models when they ran into roadblocks. They asked one AI model to create an image showing someone altering the postmark dates on mail-in ballots; it did so but replaced the mail-in ballots with regular mail. The researchers then took that image and asked a different AI model to replace the regular mail with mail-in ballots. It did so without hesitation. It is easy to imagine how in the chaotic aftermath of a close election, such imagery could provide the kind of alleged evidence that skeptics could use to undermine the results, T. J. Pyche, a former election administrator who serves on the AI + Elections Clinic advisory board at Arizona State University’s Mechanics of Democracy Laboratory and as the vice president of the nonpartisan group Ready for Tuesday, told me. Paradoxically, election officials may also benefit from how skilled AI technology has become at producing fake images and video, he said. When he conducted trainings for election administrators early last year, he would show them a series of videos and ask them to identify which were authentic and which had been generated by AI. Most could do so with relative ease, even if they divulged fears that average voters might be duped. Today, little distinguishes fake images and videos from real ones. But that could reduce the believability of extreme examples of AI-generated propaganda, Pyche noted. “Something that they have going in their favor is that people don’t believe anything anymore,” he said. “People since have moved toward thinking that everything’s AI.” [ Read: The only thing capable of uniting Bernie and Bannon ] T he spread of misinformation is only one of the threats that AI poses to the electoral system. Election administrators have also warned that the risk of cyberintrusions has increased significantly now that automated agents have developed the ability to circumvent cybersecurity defenses and secretly work together to find vulnerabilities. Governmental networks have already been targeted. Last month, researchers learned that AI agents had been probing U.S.-government websites, attempting intrusions on the Education Department’s Office of Civil Rights and initiating unauthorized interactions with the Census Bureau. In Australia, OpenAI agents bypassed cybersecurity defenses and accessed several government websites this past summer, including a Medicare-statistics portal. In a statement last week apologizing for the breaches, the company revealed that the agents had accessed public and private Medicare files. OpenAI said that it had not found evidence that patient records were breached. The fact that America’s elections are so decentralized—more than 10,000 entities manage the voting process at the state and local levels—has long been hailed as a kind of defense mechanism against foreign tampering. Someone trying to flip a statewide election would presumably have to compromise the vote in multiple jurisdictions and polling locations to have a large effect on ballot totals. But many of those offices operate on limited budgets and are especially vulnerable to AI agents that can penetrate weak defenses. Several municipalities in Maine experienced cyberintrusions this past summer that forced some government services to shut down temporarily. Although AI does not appear to have been involved in the breaches, the fallout still stood as a warning about how fragile our electoral system is, Bellows said: “When cyber adversaries are targeting little tiny towns in rural Maine, we have a problem—and AI just accelerates that problem.” Geopolitical developments—the United States is at war with Iran and locked in strategic standoffs with other adversaries—only heighten the level of danger. “These kinds of sophisticated models can be integrated into activities by foreign threat actors—Iran, Russia, China all being high on that list,” Isabel Linzer, a policy analyst on the elections-and-democracy team at the Center for Democracy and Technology, told me. “It is worrying because we are, on one hand, reducing the defense capabilities, while we are also seeing an increased threat environment because the technology has advanced.” Donald Trump, who last week met with the CEOs of several top AI companies, has downplayed the risks. The president suggested that he is not interested in implementing new federal restrictions on a technology that he asserted “will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution.” He said that the companies are doing “tremendous self-policing” and previously claimed that the only guardrail AI needs is a “STRONG AND SMART” president. The Trump administration has been especially hostile to efforts by state and local election administrators to protect themselves against cyberintrusions. The main agency responsible for shielding election systems from cyberthreats, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, has been decimated by staff cuts and dysfunction since Trump’s return to office. CISA’s work on election security has been scaled back significantly as well. Meanwhile, Trump has continued to prime his supporters with misinformation about elections, repeatedly calling voting in America “rigged” and vulnerable to wide-scale fraud. The White House did not respond to a request for comment on the record. A White House official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told me that the Trump administration will ensure that the upcoming elections are free and fair. A spokesperson for CISA did not respond to a request for comment. [ Read: How Trump left America vulnerable to cyberattacks ] Norden, the Brennan Center official, said that his team got in touch with companies to discuss fixes after his research identified flaws in their models’ handling of election misinformation. A Google spokesperson pointed me to a September 9 blog post in which the company outlined measures it had implemented to shore up its cybersecurity defenses ahead of the midterms. Other AI companies have touted similar election-security programs, including special watermarks that help flag AI-generated content. Nate Evans, a spokesperson for OpenAI, referenced the company’s own watermark program in a statement. “Our goal is to support people’s ability to participate freely in elections and make their own decisions with reliable information and effective safeguards,” he told me. “On cyber, we are also working closely with cyber defenders across the elections ecosystem and we continue to monitor for cyber abuse.” A Meta spokesperson pointed me to a February blog post showing how the company is preparing for the midterms. An Anthropic spokesperson sent me the company’s April 24 blog post on the company’s “election safeguards.” Spokespeople for xAI, Perplexity, and DeepSeek—all of which were tested in the Brennan study—did not respond to my requests for comment. AI could help with parts of the electoral process that can be monotonous and time-consuming, some officials told me. Bill Gates, a former Maricopa County supervisor who now leads Arizona State University’s Mechanics of Democracy Laboratory, told me that he has been working with election officials to find ways to use AI to reduce redundancy and increase efficiency. “There are these sort of tedious tasks that exist in elections—tedious but extremely important,” he said, referencing things such as translating material into foreign languages and creating real-time social-media updates. “To the extent that AI can be of help there, that’s wonderful.” Shortly before the 2024 election, researchers trained an “AI tutor” to provide truthful information about election administration. When election skeptics participating in a study learned facts about election administration and interacted with the chatbot, they were more likely to soften or reverse their views about alleged voter fraud in the 2020 presidential race, Adam Berinsky, an MIT professor who helped run the study , told me. Berinsky acknowledged that “in the real world,” it might be difficult to persuade a large number of Trump supporters to spend time engaging with a chatbot that rejects their preconceived notions about the voting system. Election skeptics have plenty of alternative AI options to choose from—including one that bears the imprimatur of the U.S. government. Last week, Trump unveiled America.gov , a chatbot designed to offer Americans a centralized place to ask questions about the government and its services. A day after the chatbot was unveiled, I logged on and asked whether the 2020 presidential election had been “rigged,” as Trump claims. It demurred. “I can’t say whether the 2020 presidential election was ‘rigged,’” it responded, declining to offer a “political judgment.” It gave similar answers when I asked whether Joe Biden’s victory was legitimate, whether evidence of widespread fraud existed, whether mail-in ballots had been compromised, and whether any judges had backed up Trump’s claims that the election had been stolen. When I posed those same questions this week, the chatbot seemed to have gotten smarter—or at least slightly more responsible. It noted that federal agencies have reported that the 2020 federal elections were secure, that courts dismissed Trump’s claims of fraud after the election, and that there was no widespread evidence of ballot tampering. Still, America’s chatbot stopped short of confirming that the 2020 election was free and fair, saying, “That is political commentary, which I do not provide.”

items.title: Sahara : Staffan de Mistura identifie deux obstacles majeurs
items.description: Le Conseil de sécurité des Nations unies a tenu, jeudi à huis clos, une réunion consacrée à l’évolution du dossier du Sahara marocain, marquée par les briefings de l’Envoyé personnel du secrétaire général de l’ONU, Staffan de Mistura, et du chef de la MINURSO, Alexander Ivanko. Les deux hommes ont présenté leurs appréciations et les développements sur le terrain. Ces échanges interviennent à l'approche du 31 octobre, date à laquelle le mandat de la mission onusienne MINURSO arrive à expiration et le Conseil de sécurité doit se prononcer sur son renouvellement, et alors que les discussions portent sur les perspectives du processus politique et les conditions d’une relance des négociations entre les parties. Devant les membre du Conseil de sécurité, Staffan de Mistura a présenté des documents contenant ses recommandations et les conclusions de ses derniers échanges avec les parties au conflit, dans le cadre des efforts visant à faire avancer le processus politique vers une solution consensuelle, a indiqué une source onusiennes à Hespress . En ce sens, le diplomate italo-suédois a indiqué avoir identifié deux principaux obstacles à l’avancement du processus politique, dont le premier concerne la poursuite des incidents de tirs et le non-respect de l’accord de cessez-le-feu signé en 1991. Le second obstacle évoqué, concerne de son côté, le manque de confiance entre les parties, qui empêche de réunir les conditions nécessaires à une véritable percée et à des avancées concrètes dans les négociations. Dans ce contexte, Staffan de Mistura a souligné la nécessité de s’attaquer à ces obstacles tout en poursuivant les efforts diplomatiques, avec le soutien direct du Conseil de sécurité des Nations unies. La même source a indiqué que De Mistura a souligné la poursuite de la coordination avec les États-Unis, chargés de la rédaction des textes du Conseil concernant le dossier du Sahara, afin de surmonter les difficultés et de faire progresser le processus politique. Ces éléments cité par l'Envoyé personnel, concordent avec le contenu du rapport du secrétaire général des Nations unies, António Guterres, publié le 1er octobre courant sous la référence S/2026/781. Ce document porte sur l’évolution de la situation sur le terrain et les démarches politiques entreprises à la suite de l’adoption, par le Conseil de sécurité, de la résolution 2797 en 2025. Le rapport de Guterres recommande à cet effet la poursuite des efforts de son Envoyé personnel, le renforcement des mesures de confiance entre les parties prenantes au différend régional autour du Sahara, ainsi que la prévention contre les actions de nature à compromettre le processus politique en cours. The post Sahara : Staffan de Mistura identifie deux obstacles majeurs appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Gov’t suspends implementation of L.I. restricting preaching and hawking in moving vehicles
items.description: The government has suspended implementation of the Legislative Instrument (L.I.) that prohibits preaching and hawking in moving public service vehicles, MyJoyOnline.com has learnt. The decision was confirmed to MyJoyOnline.com by a high-ranking government source, following public debate over the restrictions and concerns raised by religious leaders and other stakeholders. The regulation had attracted criticism over its implications for religious expression and evangelism in commercial vehicles, particularly the provision barring preaching and hawking while public service vehicles are in motion. The suspension is expected to allow further consideration of the measure and the concerns surrounding its implementation. However, the government has yet to publicly provide further details on the suspension or indicate when a decision on the regulation will be communicated. The Road Traffic Regulations, 2026 (L.I. 2519) prohibit causing or permitting a nuisance, including preaching and hawking, on a public or commercial vehicle while it is in motion. Under Regulation 141, an offender faces a fine of between 10 and 50 penalty units, imprisonment for up to eight months, or both. With one penalty unit valued at GH¢12, the fine ranges from GH¢120 to GH¢600. The provision means that activities sometimes seen in tro-tros and buses, including religious preaching and the sale of goods to passengers while a vehicle is moving, can attract criminal penalties. Read Also: Rev. Kwadwo Bempah defies restriction on preaching on buses; warns it won’t succeed What has changed? The restriction itself is not new. Regulation 116 of L.I. 2180 already prohibited a person from causing or permitting a nuisance, including preaching and hawking, on a public or commercial vehicle in motion. The significant change under Regulation 141 of L.I. 2519 is the tougher punishment. Under the old rules, an offender faced a fine of up to 50 penalty units, a prison term or both. The new regulations retain a fine range of 10 to 50 penalty units but raise the maximum custodial sentence to eight months. The change comes as the government steps up efforts to improve discipline and safety on the country’s roads. The Minister for Transport, Joseph Bukari Nikpe, launched a nationwide public education campaign in September to familiarise road users and transport operators with the Road Traffic (Amendment) Act, 2025 (Act 1153), and L.I. 2519. The Ministry of Transport says the new framework is intended to strengthen road safety, improve enforcement and ensure that road users understand their responsibilities. Other reforms include automated traffic enforcement, a demerit-point system linked to driving licences and tougher penalties for certain traffic offences. Why preaching and hawking are covered The regulation applies to the specified activities when a public or commercial vehicle is moving. It covers preaching and hawking as forms of nuisance and is not directed at any particular religion. The restriction also applies to people who sell goods to passengers inside moving commercial vehicles. The renewed public attention on the provision has triggered debate about religious expression, the everyday culture of public transport and the enforcement of traffic rules. However, the fact that the prohibition has existed since 2012 means the new regulations should not be interpreted as introducing an entirely new ban. Rather, they increase the possible consequences for those who breach it. The nationwide sensitisation campaign is intended to help drivers, passengers, transport operators and other road users understand the revised legal framework and comply with the rules.

items.title: Sachets interdits, bouteilles partout : Conakry face au même problème
items.description: Dans les rues de Conakry, le plastique n’a pas disparu. Il a simplement changé de forme. Depuis le 20 septembre 2026, plusieurs produits en plastique à usage unique sont interdits en Guinée, notamment les sachets destinés au conditionnement et à la vente d’eau. À travers cette mesure, les autorités entendent lutter contre la pollution et préserver les ouvrages d’assainissement. Mais quelques semaines après son entrée en vigueur, le constat dans plusieurs quartiers de la capitale soulève des interrogations. Dans les caniveaux, sur les trottoirs et aux abords des commerces, les déchets continuent de s’accumuler. Parmi eux, les bouteilles en plastique restent particulièrement visibles. Pour certains habitants, le changement se remarque surtout dans la nature des déchets qui jonchent les rues. « Avant, on voyait beaucoup de sachets d’eau dans les caniveaux. Maintenant, ce sont surtout les bouteilles qu’on retrouve. La ville reste quand même sale », témoigne Mamadou Camara, riverain à Bambéto. Un constat partagé par Aïssatou Bah, habitante de Cosa. « L’interdiction des sachets peut être une bonne chose pour l’environnement. Mais si les bouteilles que les gens utilisent aujourd’hui sont jetées aux mêmes endroits, est-ce qu’on a vraiment réglé le problème ? », s’interroge-t-elle. Les bouteilles, nouvelles vedettes des déchets urbains Les bouteilles d’eau en plastique continuent de circuler dans la capitale. Lorsqu’elles sont composées de résine PET, elles font partie des produits exclus du champ de l’interdiction, selon les dispositions évoquées dans le cadre de cette réglementation. Pour les consommateurs, elles constituent désormais l’une des principales alternatives aux sachets d’eau. « Aujourd’hui, si tu veux acheter de l’eau, tu prends une bouteille. Mais quand tu finis, il faut trouver où la jeter. Dans certains endroits, il n’y a pas de poubelle à proximité », explique Ibrahima Soumah, rencontré à Hamdallaye. À quelques mètres d’une boutique, Fatoumata Condé, vendeuse, dit constater quotidiennement la présence de bouteilles abandonnées aux alentours. « Les gens achètent, ils boivent et parfois ils laissent les bouteilles devant la boutique. Nous, on les ramasse, mais après, il faut encore savoir où les mettre. Quand les déchets restent plusieurs jours, ça devient un problème », raconte-t-elle. Dans certains caniveaux, les bouteilles se mêlent aux autres détritus. Emportées par les eaux de pluie ou bloquées contre des amas de déchets, elles contribuent à l’encombrement des ouvrages d’assainissement. Pour Abdoul Karim Diallo, riverain à Matoto, le problème dépasse donc la seule question des sachets. « On peut interdire les sachets, mais si les déchets ne sont pas correctement collectés, la saleté va rester. Aujourd’hui, tu enlèves les sachets et tu retrouves les bouteilles. Demain, si on interdit les bouteilles, qu’est-ce qui va les remplacer ? », demande-t-il. Le problème est-il le plastique ou sa gestion ? Pour de nombreux citoyens, le débat ne se limite plus à la nature des emballages autorisés ou interdits. Il porte également sur la capacité des services compétents à assurer la collecte et le traitement des déchets produits quotidiennement dans la capitale. Car une bouteille autorisée à la vente peut devenir, quelques minutes après sa consommation, un déchet susceptible de finir dans la rue, faute de dispositif adapté pour sa collecte. « Le problème, ce n’est pas seulement ce qu’on utilise. C’est aussi ce qu’on en fait après. Si tu donnes une bouteille à quelqu’un et qu’il n’a aucun endroit où la déposer, elle peut finir dans la rue », estime Mariama Touré, habitante de Dixinn. Pour elle, l’interdiction doit s’accompagner de mesures concrètes. « Il faut des poubelles, il faut que les déchets soient ramassés régulièrement et il faut aussi apprendre aux gens à ne pas jeter partout. Sinon, on va toujours déplacer le problème », ajoute-t-elle. La réglementation interdit également le rejet, le dépôt et l’abandon de déchets plastiques dans les rues, les réseaux d’assainissement et les cours d’eau. Toutefois, la présence persistante de détritus dans les caniveaux souligne l’importance de la collecte, de l’évacuation et du traitement des déchets. « Ce qu’on veut voir, c’est une ville propre. Que ce soit un sachet ou une bouteille, si le déchet reste dans le caniveau, pour nous, le problème est toujours là », souligne Oumar Sylla, habitant de Koloma. Kadiatou Diallo insiste, pour sa part, sur la responsabilité partagée entre les autorités et les citoyens. « Les autorités doivent organiser la collecte, mais nous aussi, on doit arrêter de jeter les bouteilles dans les rues. Si chacun jette son déchet n’importe où, aucune politique ne peut fonctionner », estime-t-elle. Au-delà de l’interdiction, le défi de la salubrité L’interdiction de certains plastiques à usage unique a amorcé un changement dans les habitudes de consommation. Les sachets d’eau visés par la mesure ne sont désormais plus censés être utilisés. Mais sur le terrain, les déchets continuent de raconter une autre histoire. Les bouteilles en plastique restent très présentes dans les rues et les caniveaux, relançant le débat sur leur collecte, leur recyclage et la gestion globale des déchets urbains. Pour les citoyens rencontrés, l’enjeu consiste désormais à aller au-delà du simple remplacement d’un emballage par un autre. Il s’agit de faire en sorte que les déchets, quelle que soit leur forme, ne finissent plus dans les espaces publics. À Conakry, les caniveaux restent ainsi le révélateur d’un défi majeur : faire de l’interdiction des plastiques à usage unique un véritable levier d’assainissement, plutôt qu’un simple changement dans la nature des déchets.

items.title: Archaeologists discover ancient structure at Jandial in KP near Sirkap
items.description: A previously unstudied, ancient structure measuring nearly 100 metres long and 50 metres wide has been discovered at Jandial in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Khanpur-Taxila region. The discovery has opened “new avenues for understanding the history and urban landscape of Gandhara”, a press release said on Friday. The monument, identified as Jandial D, lies opposite the famous Ionic temple of Jandial , outside the ancient fortified city of Sirkap. First noted by Alexander Cunningham in 1864, the structure remained largely unexplored for more than a century. Workers dig at the excavation site at Jandial in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. —Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Excavations that began in mid-August 2026 revealed substantial walls, while the monument’s precise function — whether public or religious — remains under investigation. The discovery was made by the KP Archaeology Department under the Khyber PATH Project, directed by Italian archaeologist Dr Luca M. Olivieri and funded by the Italian Agency for Development Cooperation (AICS). The project is being implemented by the Italian Archaeological Mission of Ca’ Foscari University of Venice in collaboration with the KP Directorate General of Archaeology and Museums. It is supervised by KP Director General of Archaeology and Museums Dr Abdul Samad. Italian NGO ISCOS provided logistical and financial support for the project. Workers dig at the excavation site at Jandial in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. —Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Dr Abdul Samad said the discovery highlighted the archaeological potential of the Khanpur–Taxila region and the importance of continued scientific research and international collaboration, stressing the need to protect archaeological remains threatened by expanding urbanisation. He said, “The discovery at Jandial demonstrates that the archaeological landscape of KP continues to hold important historical secrets. “Our priority is to support scientific research, strengthen international partnerships and protect these irreplaceable heritage assets.” Khyber Path Director Dr Olivieri said the discovery demonstrated the “richness and unpredictability of the region’s archaeological landscape”. “Its monumental scale and strategic location raise important new questions about the ancient landscape of Sirkap and the wider Gandharan region.” The Khyber PATH project has been ongoing for a year at eight archaeological sites across KP from Swat to the Khanpur–Taxila region. Its work includes the excavation and conservation of ancient fortifications at Sirsukh and research at Bazira/Barikot, which is on UNESCO’s Tentative List .

items.title: DG ISPR says Pakistan acting as an ‘honest broker’ in US-Iran war
items.description: Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) Director General Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry has said Pakistan is acting as an “honest broker” while mediating between the United States and Iran, reiterating the commitment to a “negotiated and peaceful” outcome. The military’s spokesperson made the remarks in an interview with CNN correspondent Ivan Watson, who posted a small clip of the interview on his X account. During the interview, Lt Gen Chaudhry was asked whether Pakistan can “still play a neutral role [in the US-Iran war] when Iran has targeted Saudi Arabia in the past, with the Makkah alliance , and now you have an Iranian ally — the Houthis — attacking Saudi Arabia”. “Can Pakistan be a neutral broker?” Watson asked. In response, Lt Gen Chaudhry said: “Pakistan has been exhibiting that we are a very honest broker … everything stems from honesty. We have been very clear on where Pakistan stands with all our partners”. He recalled that when the US-Iran war began, Pakistan had openly condemned Israeli attacks on Iran and also condemned Iran’s retaliatory campaign in the Gulf. “So we have been honest about that. We don’t mince our words; we have a stake in regional peace and stability. We tell all that nobody benefits from expanding this war,” he said. Lt Gen Chaudhry said Pakistan was committed to a “negotiated and peaceful” outcome to the conflict. He stressed that the country was doing “whatever is possible, whatever is necessary so that the gap narrows”. “We want that the conflict should not expand horizontally or vertically.” In a small clip of the interview released on Wednesday, Lt Gen Chaudhry was asked about deployment of Pakistani troops in Saudi Arabia under the Makkah defence alliance. In response, he said Pakistani troops were in Saudi Arabia, adding that they had been in the kingdom “for decades” and across multiple domains. In a longer clip of the interview posted by state-run Pakistan TV on X on Friday, the military’s spokesperson said that such questions were dwelling on the operationalisation of the force. “The Makkah accord, its actualisation and whatever effects it achieves, that will be purely defensive. That’s how the partners, that’s how the principles have agreed, that’s how it is going to manifest itself,” he said. “How that will be done, which component will go there, how it will be employed, that’s for the operational commander to decide. And the operational details, because it’s a military conflict … no participating country starts disclosing how and where I am going to employ my forces,” he said. “So how and when they will be employed, you will see [for] yourself,” he said. However, Lt Gen Chaudhry hastened to add that it would be “defensive in nature”. He went on to say that under the United Nations charter, all countries had the “right to self-defence”. “It is best, that rather than the threat [manifesting] into an actual operation or a military conflict, you ward it off through collective deterrence,” he said. He went on to say that the signatories of the Makkah defence pact, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, had potent military and diplomatic capabilities. “So, then anyone who is having some funny ideas against any other will hopefully think twice, thrice or multiple times. So, that stops something terrible [from] happening. That is how collective deterrence works,” he said. The remarks by the military’s spokesperson come amid escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and as the US-Israeli war on Iran, in which Islamabad has been playing the role of a mediator, shows no signs of abating. Meanwhile, the defence pact between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, signed on Aug 7, aims to strengthen collective deterrence and empower its signatory states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all of them. On Monday, the three countries agreed to the deployment of military forces and capabilities rapidly in the kingdom during an emergency meeting of alliance in Riyadh.

items.title: Journée internationale de la Poste : le message du Dr Aminata ZERBO/SABANE
items.description: En ce 9 octobre, le Burkina Faso se joint à la communauté postale internationale pour célébrer la Journée mondiale de la poste. Loin d’être une simple commémoration, cette journée nous rappelle que la poste est bien plus qu’un service de courrier et de colis. Elle est un lien. Un lien entre les personnes de divers territoires, un lien entre les producteurs et les marchés, un lien entre les citoyens et les services auxquels ceux-ci aspirent. Un lien qui rapproche, qui facilite les échanges et qui contribue, chaque jour, à faire circuler des nouvelles, des informations, des biens, des documents et des opportunités. Le thème retenu cette année par l’Union Postale Universelle, « Un seul réseau postal, des possibilités infinies », traduit à juste titre cette vocation. À travers un réseau qui s’étend à l’échelle mondiale, la poste constitue en effet l’un des plus importants réseaux de proximité au service des populations. Mais au-delà de ses infrastructures et de ses services, elle repose sur une valeur fondamentale : la confiance. La confiance de celles et ceux qui confient à la poste leurs courriers, leurs documents, leurs marchandises et, parfois, une part de leurs projets et de leurs espoirs. Au Burkina Faso, ce thème trouve un écho tout particulier avec nos ambitions nationales de transformation économique et sociale. Notre pays a besoin de réseaux solides, accessibles et résilients pour accompagner son développement. Dans cette dynamique, le réseau postal doit pleinement prendre sa place et continuer à évoluer, à se moderniser pour répondre aux besoins nouveaux de nos populations. Cette transformation est déjà engagée. Elle se traduit notamment par le développement de nouvelles formes de proximité, à l’image des Zama Tchey, qui contribuent à étendre le maillage postal et à faire de la poste, un acteur important de l’inclusion numérique en rapprochant les services dématérialisés de l’administration publique des populations. Ces nouveaux points de contact constituent aujourd’hui l’un des visages de la modernisation et de l’extension du réseau postal burkinabè. Cette transformation se traduit également par l’actualisation du cadre légal et réglementaire du secteur, l’évolution des services financiers postaux, qui a conduit à la création de la Banque postale du Burkina Faso, ainsi que par le renforcement de l’identification et de la traçabilité des envois et des opérateurs postaux à travers le lancement prochain de la plateforme nationale de tracking. À travers ces différentes initiatives, nous faisons progressivement évoluer notre réseau postal pour le rendre plus accessible, plus moderne, plus innovant et davantage en phase avec les besoins de nos populations et les transformations de notre économie. En regardant la poste aujourd’hui, nous devons voir bien au-delà du courrier que nous recevons ou du colis que nous envoyons. Nous devons voir un réseau de possibilités. Notre ambition est de faire du réseau postal burkinabè un véritable levier de développement, d'inclusion et de souveraineté, au bénéfice de toutes les populations. Cette ambition exige de poursuivre et intensifier les efforts déjà entrepris pour étendre la couverture postale, moderniser les points de contact, améliorer la qualité des services et renforcer la capacité de nos opérateurs à répondre aux mutations du secteur. Cette ambition s'inscrit pleinement dans la vision de la Révolution Progressiste Populaire et dans les orientations du Plan RELANCE, qui placent la transformation structurelle de notre économie, l'inclusion et le développement endogène au cœur de l'action publique. Sa réalisation appelle la mobilisation de l'ensemble des acteurs de l'écosystème postal : pouvoirs publics, opérateurs postaux, partenaires techniques et financiers, travailleurs du secteur et, bien entendu, les usagers eux-mêmes. C’est par le dialogue, la coopération, l’innovation et le partage d’expériences que nous pourrons construire un réseau postal à la hauteur des aspirations de notre peuple. En cette journée particulière, je voudrais, à cet égard, saluer particulièrement les femmes et les hommes qui font vivre quotidiennement la poste dans notre pays malgré les défis auxquels ils font face. Dans les bureaux de poste comme sur le terrain, dans les services de proximité comme dans les fonctions techniques et administratives, vous contribuez à maintenir ce lien de confiance qui donne tout son sens à l’activité postale. À toutes et à tous, je voudrais exprimer ma reconnaissance pour votre engagement et votre contribution au développement de notre pays. Ensemble, faisons du réseau postal Burkinabè un réseau de confiance, de proximité et d'opportunités. Heureuse Journée mondiale de la poste à toutes et à tous. Vive la Poste burkinabè. Vive le Burkina Faso. Force et victoire à nos forces combattantes. La Patrie ou la Mort, nous Vaincrons.

items.title: Three Saudi nationals killed in Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport
items.description: Three Saudi nationals have been killed in two attacks on the international airport in the capital, Riyadh, the country’s civil aviation authority has said after Yemen’s Houthis said they targeted the facility. The attacks also resulted in “injuries to a number of Saudi citizens and residents of various nationalities”, the General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement on X. It said the first attack on Thursday targeted the airport while the second one struck an aircraft belonging to state carrier Saudia. One of its pilots was among those killed, the airline said in a statement. Air traffic had returned to normal, the civil aviation authority said. Yemen’s Houthi group said on Thursday it had attacked the airport with two missiles, reports said. The Iran-aligned group said it had also targeted an airport in Najran city near the Saudi border with Yemen, and Khamis Mushait air base further north. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed these attacks. The latest casualties follow the deaths of three people in Houthi attacks on two Saudi airports on October 6 and 7. Two were killed and 28 wounded in an attack at Abha International Airport, the civil aviation body said on Wednesday. Another person was killed at King Khalid airport. The latest attacks come amid mark an escalation in renewed fighting between Yemen’s Saudi-backed government forces and the Houthis, who control most of the country’s north-west. The Houthi military spokesperson said the previous two attacks on Saudi Arabia’s airports were in “response to the Saudi aggression against our country” which saw “60 airstrikes and missile attacks in the past 24 hours”. The group says it is targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen’s civil war. The conflict has worsened in recent weeks, after the Houthis seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive. That included the port of Mokha on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which is the narrowest point of the Red Sea and a chokepoint for global shipping. But Yemeni pro-government forces have since said they had “secured” the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea. A Saudi-led coalition was formed in 2015 after Arab countries joined forces to stop the Houthis taking over Yemen from the country’s internationally recognised government. A temporary ceasefire was brokered in 2022 after years of air strikes and ground fighting led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people, triggering one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. But the informal ceasefire began to unravel in July. The Houthis announced a “maritime embargo” against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. They said they were retaliating for what they say is a years-long Saudi blockade, and for an air strike on Sanaa airport.

items.title: En Inde, la malédiction de la dot

La dot, qui consiste à transférer des biens de la famille de la mariée à la famille du marié en échange du mariage, s’inscrit dans une société marquée par de fortes inégalités entre les sexes, où la naissance d’une fille est encore souvent perçue comme un désavantage.

Se trata de la sanción conocida más alta en España por la acción de un influencer , cuyo nombre no ha revelado el departamento de Pablo Bustinduy, pero los datos coinciden con un sorteo organizado por TheGrefg , alias del murciano David Cánovas, quien precisamente usó esa empresa en las bases legales de su rifa . EL PAÍS ha intentado recoger la versión de Cánovas —que suma casi 20 millones de suscriptores en YouTube— sin éxito. items.title: Promotion juvénile : Orange Guinée recrute neuf influenceurs comme ambassadeurs
items.description: Orange Guinée a signé, jeudi 8 octobre 2026, des contrats avec neuf influenceurs guinéens issus de trois catégories : humour, lifestyle et show. Ces créateurs de contenu rejoignent le cercle des ambassadeurs de la société de télécommunications, aux côtés de plusieurs personnalités du monde artistique et sportif. Dans le cadre de sa mission de contribution à l’épanouissement de la jeunesse, Orange Guinée renforce sa collaboration avec les créateurs de contenu locaux. La société a officialisé, ce jeudi 8 octobre à Conakry, la signature de contrats avec neuf influenceurs guinéens. Ils sont répartis en trois catégories : Karim Guipö Kaba, Diallo Piscine et Gambalou pour l’humour ; Yuyu, Crépin Lamah et El Yayus pour le lifestyle ; et Fresh DD, Tad et l’Afrique Noir ainsi qu’IKK Show pour le show. À cette occasion, chacun des nouveaux ambassadeurs a reçu un iPhone 18 et des tee-shirts offerts par la société. Ils rejoignent ainsi la famille des ambassadeurs d’Orange Guinée, qui compte notamment l’artiste Saïfon Baldé, la chanteuse Djelikaba Bintou Kouyaté, le footballeur international Serhou Guirassy et l’humoriste Kabakoudou. Prenant la parole, le directeur général d’Orange Guinée et président de la Fondation Orange Guinée, Ousmane Boly Traoré, a salué le travail accompli par ces influenceurs et la confiance dont ils bénéficient auprès de leurs communautés respectives. « Vous avez des millions de personnes qui vous suivent, que vous avez convaincues et qui ont certainement adhéré à votre discours. Vous bénéficiez d’une certaine crédibilité auprès de ces millions de personnes et, aujourd’hui, qu’Orange Guinée vienne vers vous, c’est une marque de reconnaissance par rapport à votre propre travail », a-t-il déclaré. Le responsable a également souligné la nécessité de préserver la crédibilité des créateurs de contenu dans le cadre de ce partenariat. « C’est un challenge pour nous de ne pas vous donner un message qui va vous dénigrer. Il nous appartient d’être bons dans les messages que nous voulons délivrer et dans les services que nous proposons. Il faut que vous soyez à l’aise de porter notre nom, sans pour autant nous discréditer », a expliqué Ousmane Boly Traoré. Il a, par ailleurs, exprimé le souhait de voir les influenceurs poursuivre leur travail auprès des jeunes et continuer à renforcer leur impact sur les réseaux sociaux. Évoquant les ambitions de croissance de l’opérateur, il a souhaité que les communautés numériques des influenceurs grandissent parallèlement au nombre de clients d’Orange Guinée, qu’il estime à 10 millions. De son côté, Youssouf Baldé, connue sous le pseudonyme de Yuyu, a exprimé sa joie et sa reconnaissance à la suite de cette signature. « Je suis vraiment très heureuse et très ravie d’avoir la confiance d’Orange. C’est aussi un message à toute la jeunesse : on peut naître, grandir et réussir en Guinée », a-t-elle affirmé. La créatrice de contenu s’est engagée à promouvoir des messages authentiques et à travailler avec rigueur aux côtés de l’entreprise. « Je compte apporter tout ce que je fais de plus beau, transmettre un message authentique et travailler avec Orange Guinée dans la rigueur, parce que j’ai les mêmes valeurs qu’eux : créer, inspirer et connecter », a-t-elle ajouté. Revenant sur son parcours, de son expérience de Miss à sa carrière de créatrice de contenu, Yuyu a remercié Dieu, sa famille, son équipe et sa communauté pour leur soutien. À travers ce partenariat, Orange Guinée entend s’appuyer sur la notoriété des influenceurs pour toucher davantage de jeunes, tout en misant sur la création de contenu et la proximité avec les communautés numériques. Elisa Camara L’article Promotion juvénile : Orange Guinée recrute neuf influenceurs comme ambassadeurs est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.description: Minister for Energy and Green Transition, Dr John Abdulai Jinapor, has called on agencies and institutions under his ministry to demonstrate measurable results, warning that unnecessary delays and persistent non-performance will not be tolerated. In a Facebook post on Friday, October 9, Dr Jinapor said he had engaged the leadership of the institutions to review their 2026 performance, address outstanding challenges and establish clear priorities for 2027. He highlighted progress in efforts to strengthen Ghana’s energy security, including plans to install 3,000 transformers, developments in power generation, an increase in electricity access to 89.13 per cent and renewed efforts to revitalise domestic oil refining. The Minister said the next phase of the sector’s development must focus on translating commitments into tangible outcomes, with accountability, efficiency, transparency and value for money guiding the work of every agency. items.description: (Ouagadougou, 9 octobre 2026). Le Ministre Directeur de cabinet du Président du Faso, le Camarade Capitaine Martha Céleste Anderson Dekomwin MEDAH, a remis ce jeudi 8 octobre un deuxième chèque, de plus de 125 millions FCFA issus de la distribution du Recueil de discours « Le Capitaine Ibrahim TRAORÉ a dit » et du « Manifeste de la Révolution Progressiste Populaire », au profit du Fonds de Soutien Patriotique (FSP). Cette remise intervient après le chèque de plus de 35 millions FCFA donné en juin dernier. Le Camarade Capitaine Martha Céleste Anderson Dekomwin MEDAH a salué l’engouement des Burkinabè et des amis du Burkina Faso pour ces documents qui a permis d’augmenter les ressources au profit du Fonds de Soutien Patriotique. « C’est l’occasion de renouveler notre appel aux Burkinabè et aux amis du Burkina Faso, à acquérir ces ouvrages d’une part, pour leur propre édification et d’autre part, pour contribuer indirectement au FSP », a soutenu le Camarade Ministre Directeur de cabinet du Président du Faso. Pour le Camarade Ministre de l’Économie et des Finances, Dr Aboubakar NACANABO, ce chèque d’une valeur de 125 millions 10 mille FCFA constitue l'une des plus grandes contributions de l’année 2026, et est le témoignage de l’engagement du Président du Faso, le Camarade Capitaine Ibrahim TRAORÉ, en faveur du Fonds de soutien patriotique. Ce geste venant de la plus haute institution de l’État doit être, selon le Camarade Ministre de l’Économie et des Finances, un signal fort pour les Burkinabè et l’ensemble des partenaires de notre pays. items.title: Cars torched and shops looted as anti-migrant violence erupts in South Africa
items.description: At least 24 vehicles have been set ablaze and foreign-owned shops looted in South Africa as anti-immigration protests descended into violence in two major cities, police say. Clashes broke out on Thursday in Soweto, a sprawling township outside Johannesburg, the country’s largest city, and Durban, a major port on the east coast. The violence comes amid growing anger over a court ruling requiring the government to remove barriers that had prevented some migrants from applying for asylum. South Africa has experienced repeated outbreaks of xenophobic violence, often targeting migrants from neighbouring countries. Thursday’s demonstration turned violent following allegations that a foreign national had assaulted one of the protesters in Durban. Three foreign nationals were arrested in connection with the alleged assault, police said. In Durban, in the eastern province of KwaZulu-Natal, protesters gathered outside a government refugee reception centre demanding that it stop accepting asylum applications. Police fired rubber bullets to disperse crowds as businesses in the city centre shut their doors. “There were clashes between foreign nationals in the area and South African nationals,” senior local police officer Xolani Fihla told state broadcaster SABC. “At the present moment, I can confirm that no injuries have been reported,” he added. Police said 14 vehicles were torched in Durban and 10 in Soweto, where gunshots were also reported during confrontations between residents and foreign shopkeepers. Acting national police commissioner Lt Gen Puleng Dimpane condemned the destruction of property. In Orlando West, a neighbourhood of Soweto, residents had initially gathered to demand the closure of small convenience stores, known locally as spaza shops, operated by foreign nationals. Protesters forced foreign traders out of some areas, while shops were attacked and a building was set on fire, local media reported. Police said reinforcements had been deployed to prevent further violence. The authorities have promised to pursue those responsible for the destruction. The latest unrest follows a July ruling by South Africa’s Constitutional Court, the country’s highest court, which struck down restrictions preventing some people from seeking asylum because of how they entered the country or missed immigration deadlines. The judgment means asylum seekers must be allowed to submit applications, even if they entered South Africa without the required documents. It has prompted hundreds of people to gather at refugee reception centres, fuelling anger among anti-immigration campaigners who fear the decision will encourage undocumented migration. Government spokesman William Baloyi told Reuters news agency that people had deliberately spread false claims about the judgment, creating the impression that undocumented migrants would automatically be granted legal status. Baloyi insisted that the ruling does not automatically give migrants refugee status or the right to remain permanently in South Africa. Officials say applications will still be assessed individually and applicants will remain subject to immigration checks. The protests forced tens of thousands of migrants to flee, with some returning home through repatriation programmes organised by their governments. South Africa has struggled with xenophobic attacks for nearly two decades. In 2008, more than 60 people were killed and tens of thousands displaced during widespread attacks on foreign nationals. The latest unrest comes against a backdrop of widespread poverty, deep inequality and unemployment affecting roughly a third of the workforce. Migrants are frequently accused of taking jobs, contributing to crime and placing pressure on public services, although researchers say such sweeping claims are not supported by evidence. Despite its economic difficulties, South Africa remains one of the continent’s main destinations for migrants seeking employment, safety and better opportunities.

items.title: We’ll strengthen unity and party structures to win 2028 election – John Boadu assures Kufuor
items.description: The newly elected national executives of the New Patriotic Party (NPP) have pledged to strengthen party unity and consolidate its organisational structures as they prepare for the 2028 general election. National Chairman John Boadu said this when he led the newly elected executives to call on former President John Agyekum Kufuor to formally introduce the new leadership and seek his advice. Mr Boadu said the engagement was intended to draw on the former president’s political experience and understanding of the NPP as the party begins a new chapter under its newly elected leadership. He noted that Mr Kufuor’s longstanding association with the party and commitment to its founding ideals made his counsel particularly valuable as the executives work to strengthen the party and prepare for the next electoral contest. “We recognise that his wealth of experience, deep understanding of the NPP and enduring commitment to the ideals of our great tradition remain invaluable assets to the party,” Mr Boadu said. He added that the delegation approached the meeting with humility, acknowledging the responsibilities associated with leading the party at a critical moment in its political journey. “We listened with great humility to his words of wisdom and reflected on the responsibility that comes with leading the NPP at this critical moment,” he said. Mr Boadu said the new leadership was determined to build on the party’s history while prioritising unity, stronger organisational structures and collective action towards the 2028 election. “As a new leadership, we are committed to building on the party’s rich history, strengthening our unity, deepening our structures, and working tirelessly to restore the NPP to electoral victory,” he stated. The NPP elected its new national executives at a delegates’ conference held in Kumasi on Saturday, 3 October, marking the beginning of a new phase in the party’s leadership.

items.title: Mahama’s meeting with UN financial inclusion renews focus on women’s access to finance – Joyce Bawah Mogtari
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama’s meeting with the United Nations Secretary-General’s Special Advocate for Inclusive Finance for Development, Queen Máxima of the Netherlands, has highlighted the need to strengthen women’s financial inclusion in Ghana and beyond. Senior Presidential Advisor and Aide to President Mahama, Joyce Bawah Mogtari, said the engagement on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly brought together two advocates around the need to make financial systems more responsive to women’s needs. Queen Máxima has championed efforts to expand access to financial services, strengthen institutions and improve the ability of underserved groups to participate in economic activity. “That is why the meeting between President Mahama and Queen Máxima was so significant. It brought together two strong voices around a shared question: how do we build financial systems that work better for women and, in doing so, unlock their full economic potential?” Mrs Bawah Mogtari wrote in a Facebook post on Friday, October 9. She cited data showing that 78.3% of Ghanaian women aged 15 and above had a bank or mobile money account in 2024, up from 27.1% in 2011. However, she noted that account ownership among men stood at 84.4%, while disparities in access to credit remained a concern. Mrs Bawah Mogtari said Ghana needed to improve access to affordable financing for women-owned businesses, introduce more flexible collateral requirements, expand access to patient capital and deliberately support women-led industries. She also highlighted the future of the Women’s Bank as an important part of efforts to strengthen women’s access to financial services. “Financial inclusion must remain central to our efforts to empower women, strengthen households and build sustainable economies,” she said, stressing that women’s economic empowerment should remain a priority in Ghana’s development agenda.

items.title: Vient de paraître | Les politiques de sécurité routière dans le monde arabe
items.description: Les Éditions L’Harmattan à Paris publient le 15 octobre 2026, dans la collection ‘Diplomatie et Stratégie’, une étude intitulée ‘‘La sécurité routière dans le monde arabe – Politiques et pratiques’’ , de Mohssen Ben Aïssa, ancien directeur de l’Observatoire national de la sécurité routière (ONSR) de Tunisie. L’ouvrage est préfacé par Emmanuel Caulier. Plus de 26 000 personnes perdent la vie chaque année sur les routes du monde arabe. Les jeunes adultes (notamment entre 16 et 36 ans) forment une part importante des personnes touchées par les accidents mortels. Certains pays du Golfe et de la péninsule arabique affichent des taux très élevés (par exemple en Arabie saoudite, avec plusieurs milliers de décès par an et une forte pression sur les services hospitaliers), et ce malgré des réseaux autoroutiers et des infrastructures modernes. Union arabe de la sécurité routière et diverses associations locales (comme en Tunisie) multiplient les partenariats avec des entreprises et des mouvements de jeunesse pour renforcer la formation, la prévention sur les trajets professionnels et la sensibilisation. Cependant, et alors que de nombreuses régions du monde ont réussi à réduire sensiblement leur mortalité routière, plusieurs pays arabes peinent encore à inverser la tendance, malgré des stratégies adoptées, des lois votées et des financements mobilisés. L’auteur s’interroge sur les raisons de cet écart persistant entre les intentions affichées et la réalité du terrain. Son analyse s’articule autour de trois axes : une rétrospective des politiques arabes de sécurité routière depuis 1972, une étude approfondie de l’expérience tunisienne, et une feuille de route pour une nouvelle gouvernance routière arabe, fondée sur la transformation numérique. Spécialiste des politiques de sécurité routière, Mohssen Ben Aïssa a participé à de nombreux programmes de coopération arabes et contribué à l’élaboration de la Stratégie arabe de sécurité routière. Il conjugue dans ce livre son expérience de praticien et de chercheur. I. B. ‘‘La sécurité routière dans le monde arabe – Politiques et pratiques’’ , L'Harmattan, collection Diplomatie et Stratégie, 342 pages, 35 €. EAN : 9782336644660. L’article Vient de paraître | Les politiques de sécurité routière dans le monde arabe est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Surveillance des pêches : 40 inspecteurs du CNSP formés à la navigation maritime et aux techniques d’inspection
items.description: Le Centre national de surveillance et de police des pêches (CNSP) a clôturé, jeudi 8 octobre 2026 à Conakry, la formation de son deuxième groupe d’inspecteurs. Au total, 40 agents ont bénéficié de ce programme de renforcement des capacités axé sur la navigation maritime, les techniques d’inspection et la maîtrise des instruments juridiques, dans le cadre de la lutte contre la pêche illégale. Initiée par la Direction générale du CNSP, sous l’impulsion du ministère de la Pêche et de l’Économie maritime, cette formation s’est déroulée en deux sessions : du 16 au 21 septembre pour le premier groupe et du 6 au 8 octobre pour le second. L’objectif est de renforcer les compétences techniques et juridiques des inspecteurs afin d’améliorer la surveillance des activités de pêche et la lutte contre la pêche illégale, non déclarée et non réglementée (INN). Les participants ont notamment été formés à la navigation maritime et à la sécurité nautique, aux techniques d’inspection des navires à quai et en mer, à l’identification des engins de pêche ainsi qu’à l’application des textes juridiques nationaux et internationaux encadrant les activités de pêche. Dans son discours de clôture, le directeur général du CNSP, Guillaume Hawing, a souligné que l’efficacité de la surveillance maritime ne dépend pas uniquement des équipements disponibles, mais également de la compétence et de l’intégrité des agents chargés de les utiliser. Il a particulièrement insisté sur la maîtrise des procédures d’inspection et des instruments juridiques, rappelant que chaque infraction constatée et chaque procès-verbal dressé engagent la crédibilité de l’État devant les juridictions et les partenaires internationaux. « L’efficacité du contrôle et de la surveillance ne repose pas uniquement sur l’acquisition d’équipements navals et technologiques de pointe, mais avant tout sur l’excellence, la valeur et l’intégrité des femmes et des hommes qui les mettent en œuvre. Chaque constatation d’infraction, chaque procès-verbal que vous dressez engage la crédibilité de l’État face aux juridictions et à nos partenaires internationaux », a-t-il déclaré. Le patron du CNSP a également partagé son expérience personnelle, expliquant avoir appris les réalités du métier au contact des agents. Il a salué leur engagement malgré les risques liés aux missions en mer, marquées notamment par des noyades et des pertes en vies humaines. « Quand je prenais fonction, je venais avec un bagage dont la matrice était nulle, parce que je ne connaissais rien de ce métier. Je me suis mis dans votre école, j’ai appris avec vous. Aujourd’hui, j’ai beaucoup de choses à dire, comme pour dire : à cœur vaillant, rien d’impossible », a-t-il confié. Évoquant les dangers auxquels sont exposés les inspecteurs, Guillaume Hawing a rendu hommage à ceux qui, après avoir perdu des collègues en mer, continuent d’accepter de repartir en mission. « C’est une force. Ça s’appelle la conviction, ça s’appelle le supranationalisme, ça s’appelle l’amour pour le métier. Sinon, partir en mer, voir ton ami mourir, revenir et accepter de repartir, c’est une force qui n’est pas donnée à n’importe qui », a-t-il souligné. « La vie est sacrée », a-t-il insisté, rappelant que les missions de surveillance des pêches comportent des risques importants et exigent un engagement permanent au service de la protection des ressources halieutiques guinéennes. Au nom des participants, Aboubacar Mickael Sylla, inspecteur chef de la base de surveillance de Conakry, a remercié les autorités du ministère de la Pêche et de l’Économie maritime ainsi que la Direction générale du CNSP pour les efforts consentis en faveur du perfectionnement des agents. « En tant qu’inspecteurs, nous nous engageons à mettre en pratique les acquis de cette formation dans l’exercice de nos fonctions afin de contribuer efficacement au renforcement du contrôle, de la surveillance et de la gestion durable des ressources halieutiques », a-t-il assuré. De son côté, l’inspectrice Kadiatou Bah, représentant le préfet maritime, a insisté sur l’importance d’une collaboration permanente entre les différentes structures chargées de la surveillance et de la protection des espaces maritimes guinéens. « Aucune structure ne peut, à elle seule, assurer efficacement la protection de nos espaces maritimes. Notre objectif est simple : parler d’une même voix, agir de manière coordonnée, obtenir des résultats concrets », a-t-elle déclaré, réaffirmant la disponibilité de la Préfecture maritime à collaborer avec les services compétents. En clôturant officiellement la formation du deuxième groupe, Guillaume Hawing a réaffirmé l’engagement de la Direction générale du CNSP à poursuivre les efforts visant à mettre à la disposition des inspecteurs les moyens logistiques, sécuritaires et juridiques nécessaires à l’accomplissement de leurs missions. Au-delà du renforcement des compétences individuelles, cette initiative ambitionne de consolider les capacités opérationnelles du dispositif national de surveillance des pêches et de contribuer à une gestion durable des ressources halieutiques.
